exercises.prompt: Implement average3(a, b, c) so it returns the average of the three numbers, rounded to the nearest whole number with Math.round.
hints: An average is the sum of the values divided by how many there are — three here.
(a + b + c) / 3 gives the raw mean; wrap it to snap it to a whole number.
return Math.round((a + b + c) / 3); the inner parentheses make the sum happen before the division.

exercises.prompt: Implement hypotenuse(a, b) so it returns the length of the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs a and b — the square root of a squared plus b squared — rounded to the nearest whole number with Math.round.
hints: Square each leg, add the squares, take the square root, then round — you can nest all four into one expression.
a ** 2 raises a to the power of 2, and Math.sqrt(x) is the square root of x.

exercises.prompt: Implement isEven(n) so it returns true when the integer n is even and false when it is odd. Zero is even, and negative even numbers like -2 count as even too.
hints: A number is even exactly when dividing it by 2 leaves no remainder.
The remainder operator % gives that leftover: n % 2 is 0 for evens.
return n % 2 === 0 — this stays correct for 0 and for negatives.

exercises.prompt: Implement wholeDivide(a, b) so it returns how many whole times b fits into a, discarding any remainder — integer division. For example wholeDivide(7, 2) is 3. Assume a is zero or positive and b is a positive integer.
hints: Plain division gives a decimal (7 / 2 is 3.5); you want only the whole-number part.
Math.floor(x) rounds down to the nearest integer, dropping the fractional remainder.

exercises.prompt: Implement absoluteDifference(a, b) so it returns the distance between the two numbers — how far apart they are — as a non-negative value. absoluteDifference(3, 5) and absoluteDifference(5, 3) are both 2.
hints: The distance between two numbers is their difference with any negative sign removed.
a - b might be negative; Math.abs(x) turns a negative into its positive twin and leaves positives unchanged.

exercises.prompt: Implement clampToRange(x, lo, hi) so it limits x to the range lo..hi, but this time without any if or ternary — use Math.min and Math.max. Return lo when x is below lo, hi when x is above hi, and x otherwise. Assume lo <= hi.
hints: Do it in two moves: first stop x from going above hi, then stop the result from dropping below lo.
Math.min(x, hi) caps the top; wrapping that in Math.max(lo, ...) raises the floor.
return Math.max(lo, Math.min(x, hi)) — no if needed.
